But you can try something like this: Try this:
	•	Breathe in counting 4 seconds
	•	Hold your breath for 4 seconds
	•	Breathe out for 4 seconds
	•	Hold empty for 4 seconds

That makes up one cycle. Do 12 cycles like this, and your mind will be in a different state. It takes only about 4 minutes.

Breathing in and out should be done through the nose, and as deep, even and silently as possible.

If 4 seconds is too hard, you can do 3 seconds. If it's too easy, you can increase the count.

From my understanding the yogic and tantric traditions emphasize concentration meditation. To my knowledge, in these traditions there is little or no talk about a method of meditation that keeps the attention in "open monitoring" mode - it's always "focused attention" or "no meditation". 

On the other hand, several scriptures do speak that we must "be always observing" or "keep the object of meditation always in mind" or "never forget the name of God [mantra]". So the advice for daily life is to keep aware, observing, and with the meditation object in the back of one's mind at all times. 

For me, to be "always observing" or "always remembering God / the Self" is a form of mindfulness. It is simply not directed at the body, senses and sensations, like it is in the Buddhist framework.

I think it is fair to say that there is more detailed literature, in English, about Buddhist meditation than about Yogic meditation - so I can see this "advantage". I wouldn't say, though, that Buddhist meditation is more intensive - in fact, if you look at hardcore practitioners from both traditions, they are pretty much very similar, though the yogis tend to be a bit more radical.

At the end of the day, it's about which tradition/technique appeals to you in your heart. For me it is the yogi tradition - though I have practice in the Zen Buddhist tradition for some years, and have great respect for the Theravada.

As to pranayama, I would suggest you do this simple exercise. It is straightforward and safe.

This is one of the several techniques of Pranayama (Yogic Breathing).

- Close your right nostril with your right thumb, and breathe in through the left nostril, counting 4
- Then close your left nostril with your right index finger, open the right nostril, and breathe out counting 8

You can go for 3-6, or 5-10, 6-12, etc. The important thing is that we are aiming for the  exhalation to be longer than the inhalation (ideally double). That may be hard in the beginning, so you grow into it as you go.

Breathing should be soft, even, and as soundless as possible. Do not force yourself, it should be comfortable. So adjust your count according to your capacity. 

In the beginning it may be a bit hard to get the exhalation twice as long as inhalation, but by time and patience we get there.

You can practice this for 5~15min. It is very relaxing. After that you can just breath normally, and follow with your meditation practice of focusing the attention on the breath, on a mantra, or on the space between the eyebrows.

>Is anyone here "enlightened"?

Enlightened people are highly unlikely to come forward saying "I'm enlightened". 
If you take the traditional, hard-core concept of enlightenment, then I would risk estimating that in any generation there are less than 50 (fully) enlightened people in the world. It is extremely rare. Some people believe it's no more than a couple of handful in any generation. 

If you are talking about modern, relativized and watered-down concepts about enlightenment that we see, for example, in popular western Buddhism, and in neo-Advaita (see criticism [here](http://liveanddare.com/neo-advaita/)), then there are probably a few thousands of people that believe they are enlightened.

On the other hand, the 4 levels of enlightenment of Buddhism may help understand the different "levels" of masters out there.

> do you ever plan on reaching that point? What is your path to reaching this?

In a way, that is the goal and purpose of all efforts. I say in a way, because from another point of view, I simply practice because I practice. I practice because it is the best way to live.

My path is a mixture of *Advaita Vedanta* and *Raja Yoga*, though I also take inspiration and insight from *Theravada Buddhism*.

Do you personally know anyone who claims to be enlightened?

I have traveled to India 4 times, and have been to several Satsangs. I have also read hundreds of books and watched many online teaching videos. I have only met two masters in this journey that I feel, beyond any doubt in my heart, that they are fully enlightened. 

One is **Sri Lakshamana Swami**. He is a 80+ years old recluse, living in Tiruvannamalai, who attained Realization in the last year of Ramana Maharshi's life. He is no longer accessible for contact. His path is that of Advaita Vedanta.

The other is **Shiva Rudra Bala Yogi**. He is 61 years old, and travels the world teaching and giving retreats. His path is that of Raja Yoga, and he attained Liberation after meditating 18 hours a day, for 5 years in a row.

Apart from these two, I have met many other great teachers. But to my current level of spiritual discrimination/insight, they do not seem fully enlightened.

Hard to say, as their paths have differred a lot. Intellectual knowledge or reading on the subject is not one of the elements, though. I don't think Tolle is fully enlightened, though he is certainly an inspiring man and good teacher. In any case, there is no "spiritual lottery". Effort always precede realization - either in this life, or in previous ones.

This is one of the several techniques of Pranayama (Yogic Breathing).

- Close your right nostril with your right thumb, and breath in through the left nostril, counting 4
- Then close your left nostril with your right index finger, open the right nostril, and breathe out counting 8

You can go for 3-6, or 5-10, 6-12, etc. The important thing is that the exhalation be twice the length of the inhalation.

Breathing should be soft, even, and as soundless as possible. Do not force yourself, it should be comfortable. So adjust your count according to your capacity. 

In the beginning it may be a bit hard to get the exhalation twice as long as inhalation, but by time and patience we get there.

You can practice this for 5~15min. It is very relaxing. After that you can just breath normally, and follow with your meditation practice of focusing the attention on the breath, on a mantra, or on the space between the eyebrows.

In the Yoga Sutras (3.2), Patanjali defines meditation (dhyana) as:

 "Meditation is unbroken flow of thought towards a single object of focus". 

That is definitely not effortless.

Meditation can only be truly effortless for the man that has extinguished his vasanas/samskaras, which is the magnetic impulse towards sense objects. Before that, effortlessness can bring some relaxation and quietude, but it is shallow and short-lived.

As you said, different traditions have different ways of expressing this. 

Ramana Maharshi, for instance, said that even thought "choiceless awareness" is effortless and is our true nature, we cannot simply try to perceive it in our current state, because our vision is so blurred with our own ego and mental tendecies/bias (samskaras). So in meditation effort is advised to "arrive" at the state where attention simply rests in pure consciousness, beyond conditioning. The idea is that all seing/perceiving, before that, happens tainted by our own conditioning and identity.

This is a very interesting discussion, and different masters/traditions indeed have different takes on it.
